study summary / 014

How do urban scenes relate to brain signals?

An EEG study distinguishes early visual processing from later appraisal of street images.

A street scene combines vegetation, buildings, vehicles, sky and visual geometry. Zähme and colleagues examined how these features related to brain responses and judgments.

The study

63 adults viewed urban street photographs during EEG recording and rated the scenes. The analysis considered the greenery-to-built ratio, other scene content and low-level visual features.

The findings

More greenery relative to built structures was associated with more positive appraisals and a larger early P1 response. Straight edges were associated with a stronger N1 response. Later P3 and LPP responses related to higher-level appraisal rather than basic affect. More sky and greater mean metric depth were associated with more negative appraisals within this image set.

Architectural interpretation

Street composition and geometry can be studied at different stages of visual processing. The results caution against assuming that a single feature, such as more visible sky, is always preferred.

Limits and conclusion

Participants viewed photographs rather than moving through streets. EEG responses do not demonstrate lasting brain changes or improved health. This summary is based on the published abstract and highlights, so conclusions remain limited to the reported laboratory findings.
